title: From Rajma Rice to Puran Poli: How Strangers Fed Delhi's NEET Protesters
excerpt: Volunteers from across India brought home-cooked meals, snacks, and water to sustain student protesters at Jantar Mantar, turning a political sit-in into a display of grassroots solidarity through food.
body:
• Strangers and volunteers have provided free food — from rajma rice and puran poli to pakoras and tea — to NEET protesters camped at Jantar Mantar since early June 2026.
  • CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke publicly thanked supporters, singling out a Muslim woman who brought hand-cooked meals and a CUET student's grandmother who sent puran poli from home.
  • The food solidarity drew contrast after CJP sacked spokesperson Vijeta Dahiya on July 21 for eating a burger during the Chalo Sansad march while protesters faced lathi charges.
  • Protesters alleged police cut off water supply and blocked food from entering the site on several occasions, raising human rights concerns.

Thousands of students have camped at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi for more than six weeks, protesting the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak and demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. But alongside the slogans and hunger strikes, a quieter story has unfolded: the steady stream of strangers who have shown up with home-cooked meals to keep the protesters fed.

A Community Kitchen Emerges

From the protest's early days in June, volunteers began arriving with food, water, and supplies. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke acknowledged the phenomenon on Day 6 of the sit-in, posting on X: "I would like to thank every brother, sister, and especially every mother who has been bringing home-cooked food for me. Your kindness, love, and support give us the strength to keep this movement going."

According to Livemint, Dipke shared a video of a young Muslim woman in a burqa who had traveled to Jantar Mantar specifically to deliver food she had prepared by hand. In another post, he showed an image of puran poli — a traditional Maharashtrian sweet flatbread — sent by a CUET student's grandmother.

A volunteer named Junaid told reporters he served cold water, tea, breakfast, and pakoras to protesters each morning, followed by rajma rice and curry rice for lunch. Ashu, a volunteer from Ludhiana in Punjab, said he cleaned the area around Jantar Mantar daily and carried three liters of water along with sanitizers to the site, according to Livemint.

"I would like to thank every brother, sister, and especially every mother who has been bringing home-cooked food for me."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder, in a post on X

Food as Protest, Food as Solidarity

The grassroots food support has crossed religious and regional lines. Sikh volunteers distributed food and drinking water. Farmer unions that joined the movement organized free food and water arrangements at the protest site. PTI reported that people were seen distributing food and drinking water to participants through the night as the sit-in extended into its third consecutive day.

When asked repeatedly about who funds the protest, Dipke pointed at the volunteers serving food and sarcastically called them "our George Soros," adding that he did not know many of them before the agitation began.

The community kitchen that emerged at Jantar Mantar echoes a deep tradition in Indian protest culture — from the langars of the 2020-2021 farmers' protests at Delhi's borders to informal food networks at earlier student agitations. For participants who traveled from states like Uttarakhand, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh, often at their own expense and sometimes without telling their families, the free meals were essential.

When Food Became the Controversy

The role of food at the protests took an ironic turn on July 21 when CJP sacked its spokesperson Vijeta Dahiya after videos surfaced showing him eating a burger during the Chalo Sansad march on July 20 — the same day police used baton charges and tear gas on protesters attempting to march toward Parliament.

"You hold me accountable as if it's my job to be a protester... Have you elected me?" Dahiya said in a video confrontation, according to Inshorts. CJP responded by condemning his "deeply insensitive actions" while "peaceful protestors and our team were facing brutal police violence."

The optics stung: while strangers cooked rajma rice for protesters and grandmothers sent puran poli, a movement spokesperson had slipped away for fast food as tear gas filled the air.

Denied at the Gate

Volunteers' efforts have not gone unchallenged. On multiple occasions, protesters alleged that Delhi Police cut electricity and water supply at the protest site and prevented supporters from bringing food inside. Dipke described the situation as a humanitarian concern, claiming that one bottle of water was being shared among several people. He urged authorities to allow basic necessities to reach the venue.

Protesters appealed to police, arguing that access to food and water were fundamental human needs. The restrictions were partially eased after public pressure, with drinking water access restored, though tensions over access to the site have continued.

What's Next

The Jantar Mantar protests show no signs of winding down. On July 21, protesters reclaimed the site after police dismantled the stage and tents following Monday's clashes that injured nearly 180 people. The CJP has said it will continue its anti-government protest but will avoid marching on Parliament.

For the Indian diaspora watching from abroad, the food solidarity offers a familiar emotional register. The act of cooking and carrying meals to strangers — without being asked, without expectation of repayment — is rooted in a cultural reflex that transcends the political specifics of the NEET controversy. It recalls the community response during COVID-19, the farmers' agitation, and countless earlier movements where food became both sustenance and statement.

As India's monsoon session of Parliament gets underway and the CJP's demands remain unmet, the volunteers at Jantar Mantar continue to show up each day — not with placards or slogans, but with dabbas and thermoses.
image_caption: Volunteers prepare plates for a community meal. At Delhi's Jantar Mantar, strangers and volunteers have sustained NEET protesters with home-cooked meals, tea, and water for over six weeks.
